chunks: "A boost converter is a switching DC-DC converter that takes a lower input voltage and produces a higher output voltage.
It's built from an inductor, a switch, a diode and an output capacitor. The way it gets the voltage up is that the inductor does the work.
While the switch is on, the inductor is connected across the input to ground, so its current ramps up and it stores energy in its magnetic field. Then the switch turns off.
The inductor current can't just stop, so the inductor flips its voltage polarity and keeps pushing current, now through the diode into the output.
Because the inductor is in series with the input at that point, its voltage adds on top of V in , and the output sits above the input.
Averaged over a cycle, the inductor can't gain or lose volt-seconds, which gives V out equals V in over (1-D) .
At 50% duty you get double the input, at 75% you get four times, in the ideal case. It isn't free energy though.
Power in is about equal to power out, so if the output voltage is higher, the input current has to be higher too, by a factor of 1 over (1-D) .
That's why boosts get stressed at low V in and high load."
